title: Introduction to Signal Processing, Second Edition
topics: Chapter 1, Sampling and Reconstruction (physical PDF pp. 24-84; printed pp. 1-61): end-to-end analog-to-digital-to-analog processing and the sampling theorem.
Secs. 1.2-1.3: analog sinusoidal/Fourier descriptions, bandlimited signals, Nyquist rate and frequency, antialiasing prefilters, and hardware sampling-rate limits.
Sec. 1.4: sampling of sinusoids, analog reconstruction aliases, rotational/stroboscopic analogies, and conversions among Hz, radians/sample, cycles/sample, and normalized frequency.
Sec. 1.5: DTFT spectra of sampled signals, Poisson spectrum replication, and practical antialias filter transition bands.
Sec. 1.6: ideal interpolation, staircase/zero-order-hold reconstruction, spectral images, sinc droop, equalization, and analog anti-image postfilters.
Secs. 1.7-1.8 and Problems: the five-component DSP chain, theory of bandlimited functions, and 25 sampling/reconstruction exercises.
Chapter 2, Quantization (physical PDF pp. 85-118; printed pp. 62-95): uniform quantization, converter architectures, oversampling, noise shaping, and dither.
Sec. 2.1: B-bit uniform quantization, rounding and truncation, clipping, quantization-error statistics, dynamic range, SNR, and limits of the additive-white-noise model.
Sec. 2.2: oversampling, decimation, first- and higher-order error feedback, in-band noise power, and effective-bit gains.
Secs. 2.3-2.4: D/A number representations and resistor networks; counter, tracking, successive-approximation, and flash A/D converters.
Sec. 2.5 and Problems: analog and digital dither, subtractive versus nonsubtractive schemes, error whitening, and converter-design exercises.
Chapter 3, Discrete-Time Systems (physical PDF pp. 119-142; printed pp. 96-119): input/output rules and LTI-system fundamentals.
Secs. 3.1-3.3: system rules, linearity, time invariance, impulse decomposition, impulse response, and the convolution sum.
Secs. 3.4-3.5: FIR versus IIR systems, difference equations, causality, BIBO stability, delay of finitely anticausal systems, and stable approximations to anticausal tails.
Sec. 3.6: problems classifying nonlinear and time-varying operators and deriving impulse responses and convolution outputs.
Chapter 4, FIR Filtering and Convolution (physical PDF pp. 143-212; printed pp. 120-189): block and real-time sample processing.
Secs. 4.1.1-4.1.6: direct convolution, convolution tables, LTI superposition, Toeplitz matrix forms, and flip-and-slide evaluation.
Secs. 4.1.7-4.1.10: input-on/input-off transients, infinite sequences, implementation details, and overlap-add block convolution.
Sec. 4.2: numerical approximation of continuous-time convolution and experiments separating transient from steady-state behavior.
Sec. 4.3: pure delays, tapped-delay-line FIR realizations, sample-update algorithms, DSP hardware timing, and circular buffers.
Sec. 4.4: analytic, programming, and realization problems, including transposed FIR structures.
Chapter 5, z-Transforms (physical PDF pp. 213-246; printed pp. 190-223): a concise review used as a filter-analysis tool.
Secs. 5.1-5.3: transform properties, regions of convergence, poles and zeros, causality, stability, and time support.
Sec. 5.4: the DTFT as the unit-circle z-transform, inverse DTFT, Parseval, Hermitian symmetry, and geometric pole-zero evaluation.
Secs. 5.5-5.6: inverse transforms by partial fractions, ROC-dependent sequences, unilateral transforms, initial conditions, and recurrence solutions.
Sec. 5.7: problems on ROC logic, inverse transforms, modulation, Parseval, and pole-zero geometry.
Chapter 6, Transfer Functions (physical PDF pp. 247-292; printed pp. 224-269): equivalent filter descriptions, sinusoidal response, pole-zero design, and inversion.
Secs. 6.1-6.2: transfer functions connected to frequency response, difference equations, convolution, impulse response, poles/zeros, and realizations.
Sec. 6.3: steady-state sinusoidal eigenfunction response, switched-on/off transients, dominant-pole settling time, and effective duration.
Sec. 6.4: first-order filters, resonators, parametric equalizers, notch filters, and arbitrary comb filters designed directly with poles and zeros.
Sec. 6.5: deconvolution, inverse filters, causal versus anticausal stable inverses, delayed finite approximations, and noise amplification.
Sec. 6.6: problems spanning filter characterization, transient analysis, resonator design, comb filters, and stable inverse approximation.
Chapter 7, Digital Filter Realizations (physical PDF pp. 293-353; printed pp. 270-330): direct, canonical, transposed, state-space, and cascade forms.
Secs. 7.1-7.3: direct form I, canonical direct form II, signal-flow-graph transposition, memory counts, and finite-precision behavior.
Sec. 7.4: state-space realization, state-transition formulas, transfer functions, impulse responses, and transposed state-space systems.
Secs. 7.5-7.6: factoring real rational filters into first- and second-order cascade sections and converting cascade form to canonical form.
Sec. 7.7: circular addressing, FIR/IIR instruction counts, real-time sampling-rate bounds, and pipelined multiprocessor realizations.
Sec. 7.8: realization and implementation problems, including reverberators and alternative equivalent block diagrams.
Chapter 8, Lattice Realizations (physical PDF pp. 354-383; printed pp. 331-360): lattice/ladder structures and finite-word robustness.
Secs. 8.1-8.3: standard, rearranged, and normalized lattice sections; reflection coefficients; ladder taps; and cross-domain applications.
Secs. 8.4-8.6: forward/backward Levinson transformations, direct-to-lattice conversion, sample processing, and lattice frequency response.
Sec. 8.7: Schur recursion and the Schur-Cohn stability test in terms of reflection-coefficient magnitudes.
Secs. 8.8-8.10: lattice examples, coefficient-quantization sensitivity, and experiments comparing direct, cascade, and normalized-lattice realizations.
Chapter 9, DTFT and Spectral Analysis (physical PDF pp. 384-432; printed pp. 361-409): deterministic and random-signal spectrum estimation.
Secs. 9.1-9.2: finite-record windowing, leakage, frequency resolution, DTFT evaluation, equivalent Nyquist intervals, Horner evaluation, and selective-frequency detection.
Secs. 9.3-9.4: 3-dB width, Rayleigh resolution, sidelobe depth, bias, and rectangular, Hamming, Kaiser, DPSS, and Dolph-Chebyshev windows.
Sec. 9.5: Fourier-optics and spatial-array dualities, including apertures, diffraction, beam patterns, spatial sampling, and grating lobes.
Sec. 9.6: autocorrelation and power spectra, the periodogram's inconsistency, segment averaging, Welch overlap, lag-window smoothing, and resolution-variance tradeoffs.
Sec. 9.7: strictly stable filtering of wide-sense stationary signals, output PSD, noise-reduction ratio, and the random-walk failure of an ideal accumulator.
Secs. 9.8-9.9: a 309-year sunspot periodogram experiment and problems on windows, line detection, array factors, and random-signal filtering.
key_results: Secs. 1.3-1.3.1 (physical PDF pp. 31-35; printed pp. 8-12): a signal bandlimited to fmax is determined by samples at fs >= 2fmax; 2fmax is the Nyquist rate and fs/2 the Nyquist frequency.

Secs. 1.3.2-1.3.3 (physical PDF pp. 35-38; printed pp. 12-15): real signals require an analog antialias prefilter, while processing hardware imposes the complementary upper bound; a feasible design must satisfy 2fmax <= fs <= fproc.

Sec. 1.4.1 (physical PDF pp. 39-41; printed pp. 16-18): sampled sinusoids whose analog frequencies differ by integer multiples of fs have identical samples; ideal reconstruction selects the unique alias in [-fs/2, fs/2].

Secs. 1.5.1-1.5.2 (physical PDF pp. 46-51; printed pp. 23-28): the DTFT is periodic with fs in physical-frequency units, and sampling replicates the analog spectrum at every integer multiple of fs according to the Poisson summation formula.

Secs. 1.6.1-1.6.3 (physical PDF pp. 58-70; printed pp. 35-47): ideal reconstruction is sinc interpolation; a zero-order hold adds half-sample linear phase and sinc-amplitude droop, which may be digitally equalized before an analog postfilter removes images.

Sec. 1.7 (physical PDF pp. 70-73; printed pp. 47-50): a practical DSP chain separates five roles: analog antialias prefilter, A/D converter, digital processor, D/A converter (optionally equalized), and analog anti-image postfilter.

Sec. 2.1 (physical PDF pp. 86-94; printed pp. 63-71): for a B-bit uniform converter of full-scale range R, Q=R/2^B; rounded error lies in [-Q/2,Q/2], and under the busy-signal model it has mean zero, variance Q^2/12, and RMS Q/sqrt(12).

Sec. 2.1 (physical PDF pp. 94-98; printed pp. 71-75): quantizer dynamic range grows by approximately 6B dB; the additive-white-noise model is useful for wide-amplitude, rapidly varying signals but fails visibly for small or slowly varying inputs.

Sec. 2.2 (physical PDF pp. 98-104; printed pp. 75-81): unshaped oversampling by L gains one-half effective bit per doubling, whereas pth-order noise shaping makes the asymptotic gain (p+1/2)log2(L), minus an order-dependent constant.

Secs. 2.3-2.4 (physical PDF pp. 104-111; printed pp. 81-88): successive-approximation A/D conversion needs B binary-search decisions for B bits; a counter may need up to 2^B steps, while a flash converter trades speed for 2^B-1 parallel comparators.

Sec. 2.5 (physical PDF pp. 111-116; printed pp. 88-93): nonsubtractive triangular dither is the practical all-purpose choice for decorrelating quantization error; subtractive rectangular dither makes error independent without an SNR penalty but requires reproducing the same dither at decoding.
Secs. 3.2-3.3 (physical PDF pp. 123-130; printed pp. 100-107): an LTI system is completely characterized by its impulse response, and its output is the convolution y(n)=sum_k h(k)x(n-k).

Secs. 3.4-3.5 (physical PDF pp. 130-138; printed pp. 107-115): FIR systems have finite impulse responses and can be nonrecursive; IIR systems have infinite responses and commonly use feedback difference equations. Causality is h(n)=0 for n<0, and BIBO stability is equivalent to absolute summability of h.

Sec. 3.5 (physical PDF pp. 138-140; printed pp. 115-117): a stable anticausal tail may be clipped before -D and delayed to obtain a practical causal approximation; for |x(n)|<=A, the error is bounded by A times the discarded absolute tail.

Secs. 4.1.1-4.1.6 (physical PDF pp. 145-158; printed pp. 122-135): convolving lengths Lx and Lh gives length Lx+Lh-1, and direct, tabular, LTI, Toeplitz-matrix, and flip-and-slide forms are algebraically identical views of the same operation.

Secs. 4.1.7 and 4.1.10 (physical PDF pp. 158-167; printed pp. 135-144): finite convolution naturally splits into input-on transient, steady overlap, and input-off transient; overlap-add extends block convolution to very long or unbounded streams by summing shifted block outputs.

Secs. 4.3.2-4.3.4 (physical PDF pp. 178-188; printed pp. 155-165): a real-time FIR filter is a dot product against a tapped delay line; updating the state in the wrong order destroys needed samples, while circular buffering changes a pointer instead of shifting the entire state.

Secs. 5.1-5.3 (physical PDF pp. 214-223; printed pp. 191-200): linearity, delay, and convolution map naturally into z-domain algebra, but a rational expression is not a complete transform without its ROC; causal, anticausal, and two-sided sequences occupy exterior, interior, and annular ROCs.

Sec. 5.3 (physical PDF pp. 221-223; printed pp. 198-200): stability requires the ROC to contain the unit circle; therefore a stable causal rational system has all poles inside it, while a stable anticausal system has all poles outside it.

Sec. 5.4 (physical PDF pp. 223-231; printed pp. 200-208): the DTFT is X(z) evaluated on z=exp(jomega); Parseval equates time-domain energy with integrated spectral energy, and pole/zero distances give a geometric construction of magnitude and phase.

Sec. 5.5 (physical PDF pp. 231-237; printed pp. 208-214): partial fractions recover a rational sequence only after the ROC chooses the right- or left-sided term associated with each pole; among the admissible ROCs, exactly one containing the unit circle yields the stable inverse.

Sec. 5.6 (physical PDF pp. 237-242; printed pp. 214-219): the unilateral z-transform incorporates initial conditions directly and converts causal recurrences into algebraic equations without separately adding a zero-input response.

Secs. 6.1-6.2 (physical PDF pp. 248-252; printed pp. 225-229): transfer function, frequency response, realization, difference equation, pole-zero pattern, impulse response, and convolution equation are seven equivalent filter descriptions; design proceeds from desired H(omega) to H(z) to a realization.
Sec. 6.3.1 (physical PDF pp. 252-255; printed pp. 229-232): complex sinusoids are LTI eigenfunctions, so the steady-state response multiplies amplitude by |H(omega)| and adds phase arg H(omega).

Sec. 6.3.2 (physical PDF pp. 255-260; printed pp. 232-237): switching on a sinusoid adds pole-governed transients; if rho is the largest pole magnitude, an epsilon settling estimate is neff=ln(epsilon)/ln(rho), exposing the cost of poles close to the unit circle.

Sec. 6.4.2 (physical PDF pp. 263-270; printed pp. 240-247): a conjugate pole pair at radius R and angle omega0 creates a resonator with approximate 3-dB width Delta omega approximately 2(1-R); narrower bandwidth therefore means slower transient decay.

Secs. 6.4.2-6.4.3 (physical PDF pp. 267-274; printed pp. 244-251): paired pole-zero sections create boost, cut, or notch equalizers, while arbitrary harmonic combs place unit-circle zeros at rejection frequencies and slightly contracted poles at the same angles to control width.

Sec. 6.5 (physical PDF pp. 274-283; printed pp. 251-260): inverse filtering swaps zeros and poles; zeros outside the unit circle force a stable inverse to be anticausal, and delayed truncation can make it implementable, but inversion may amplify measurement noise severely.

Secs. 7.1-7.2 (physical PDF pp. 294-306; printed pp. 271-283): direct form II commutes numerator and denominator subfilters and merges their equal delay chains, reducing storage from separate input/output histories to K=max(M,L) delays.

Sec. 7.3 (physical PDF pp. 306-309; printed pp. 283-286): transposing a signal-flow graph reverses branches, swaps inputs and outputs, and preserves the transfer function; transposed structures can improve overflow and coefficient-quantization behavior.
Sec. 7.4 (physical PDF pp. 309-317; printed pp. 286-294): for s(n+1)=As(n)+Bx(n), y(n)=Cs(n)+Dx(n), H(z)=C(zI-A)^(-1)B+D and h(n)=CA^(n-1)B u(n-1)+D delta(n); transposition maps A,B,C to A^T,C^T,B^T.

Secs. 7.5-7.6 (physical PDF pp. 317-329; printed pp. 294-306): real rational filters decompose into first- and second-order cascade sections, but pole-zero pairing and section ordering are not unique and materially affect finite-precision noise and overflow.

Sec. 7.7 (physical PDF pp. 329-340; printed pp. 306-317): circular buffers make delay-line maintenance constant-cost; an FIR of order M needs roughly M+1+C instructions per sample and a K-biquad IIR roughly 5K+C, turning instruction time into a maximum real-time fs.

Secs. 8.1-8.3 (physical PDF pp. 355-363; printed pp. 332-340): lattice/ladder filters realize rational H(z) using reflection coefficients gamma and ladder taps; normalized sections use tau=sqrt(1-gamma^2), keep internal branch gains below unity, and improve roundoff/overflow robustness.

Sec. 8.4 (physical PDF pp. 363-370; printed pp. 340-347): forward and backward Levinson recursions map denominator coefficients to and from reflection coefficients, while a corresponding triangular recursion maps the numerator into ladder coefficients.

Sec. 8.7 (physical PDF pp. 374-376; printed pp. 351-353): the Schur-Cohn criterion gives a recursion-only stability test: a causal polynomial denominator is stable iff every extracted reflection coefficient satisfies |gamma_p|<1.

Secs. 8.9-8.10 (physical PDF pp. 377-383; printed pp. 354-360): roots of high-order direct-form polynomials can move dramatically under small coefficient perturbations, especially when clustered; cascade or normalized-lattice realizations retain stability much better in the book's quantization experiments.

Sec. 9.1 (physical PDF pp. 385-394; printed pp. 362-371): multiplying by a finite record window convolves the ideal spectrum with the window spectrum, replacing lines by mainlobes and sidelobes; for a rectangular length-L record, resolvability requires Delta f >= fs/L.

Sec. 9.1 (physical PDF pp. 389-391; printed pp. 366-368): a Hamming window suppresses first sidelobes from 13.26 dB to about 42.67 dB but roughly doubles mainlobe width; resolution lost to a wider window can be recovered only with a longer record.

Secs. 9.2-9.3 (physical PDF pp. 395-401; printed pp. 372-378): the DTFT is a polynomial evaluated on the unit circle and may be computed at selected frequencies by Horner's rule; two lines are resolved when separated by roughly the window's 3-dB width, but a weak line also must exceed leakage from stronger neighbors.

Sec. 9.3 (physical PDF pp. 399-401; printed pp. 376-378): the DPSS window maximizes energy concentration inside a prescribed mainlobe band, while the Dolph-Chebyshev window minimizes mainlobe width for a prescribed equal-sidelobe level.

Sec. 9.6 (physical PDF pp. 418-423; printed pp. 395-400): the ordinary periodogram is asymptotically unbiased but inconsistent because its variance does not vanish; averaging K segment periodograms typically reduces variance by K, at the cost of shorter-segment resolution.

Sec. 9.6 (physical PDF pp. 422-423; printed pp. 399-400): Welch uses usually 50%-overlapping segments; lag-window smoothing instead windows the sample autocorrelation, which convolves and smooths the ordinary periodogram in frequency.

Sec. 9.7 (physical PDF pp. 424-426; printed pp. 401-403): a strictly stable LTI filter maps a WSS input PSD to Syy(omega)=|H(omega)|^2 Sxx(omega); for white input, the noise-reduction ratio is sigma_y^2/sigma_x^2=integral |H|^2 d omega/(2pi)=sum_n h(n)^2.

Sec. 9.7 (physical PDF pp. 425-426; printed pp. 402-403): an ideal accumulator driven by white noise is a nonstationary random walk with variance (n+1)sigma_x^2; moving the pole to rho<1 creates a leaky integrator and restores strict stability.
pedagogy: This shard is a computationally minded first course that repeatedly moves from physical motivation to equations, plots, worked numerical examples, C/MATLAB algorithms, and substantial end-of-chapter exercises. Sampling is introduced through aliasing demonstrations, rotating-wheel intuition, and a complete converter/reconstructor chain before discrete-time system theory is formalized. Convolution is deliberately computed five ways so learners can connect superposition, geometry, matrices, hand calculation, and implementation; later chapters reuse that multi-representation habit for z transforms, transfer functions, block diagrams, state space, cascade, and lattice structures. Many sections end in executable experiments: quantization histograms and correlations, dithered low-level sinusoids, continuous-time convolution approximations, filter coefficient quantization, and sunspot spectra. The text assumes Fourier-series/transform familiarity and explicitly assumes basic z-transform familiarity in Chapter 5; matrix algebra, complex numbers, and elementary random-process concepts become increasingly important. Exercises mix derivations, numerical design, visual pole-zero reasoning, C routines, MATLAB experiments, and hardware timing. Historical DSP-chip details are dated, but their cycle-budget calculations still make real-time constraints concrete. A useful course adaptation would keep the physical examples and experiments while translating legacy code and hardware figures into modern notebooks and measured runtime labs.
figures: Recreate the five-stage DSP chain (Secs. 1.1 and 1.7, physical PDF pp. 24-25 and 70-73): analog prefilter, sampler/quantizer, digital processor, equalized D/A, and analog postfilter, with spectra beneath each stage.

Recreate the alias family and rotating-wheel analogy (Sec. 1.4, physical PDF pp. 39-46): several continuous sinusoids or rotations passing through identical samples, mapped into the symmetric Nyquist interval.
Recreate spectrum replication under sampling (Sec. 1.5.2, physical PDF pp. 49-53): a baseband analog spectrum copied at multiples of fs, first separated and then overlapping under undersampling.

Recreate ideal versus staircase reconstruction (Sec. 1.6, physical PDF pp. 58-70): sinc interpolation beside zero-order-hold steps, with the hold's phase delay, sinc droop, and spectral images aligned underneath.
Recreate the quantizer-error experiment (Sec. 2.1, physical PDF pp. 92-98): transfer staircase, error sawtooth, histogram, autocorrelation, and spectrum contrasting fine and coarse quantization.

Recreate the oversampling/noise-shaping ladder (Sec. 2.2, physical PDF pp. 98-104): flat versus first-/higher-order error spectra, retained baseband area, and effective bits versus oversampling ratio.

Recreate the dither comparison (Sec. 2.5, physical PDF pp. 111-116): the same sub-LSB sinusoid without dither and with rectangular/triangular dither, showing harmonic spurs becoming a broadband floor.

Recreate a system-property test bench (Chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 119-141): several input/output rules classified for linearity, time invariance, causality, memory, and stability, with one counterexample per failed property.

Recreate the five views of one convolution (Secs. 4.1.2-4.1.6, physical PDF pp. 146-158): direct sums, convolution table, shifted impulse responses, Toeplitz matrix, and flip-and-slide animation using the same short sequences.
Recreate the convolution phase map (Sec. 4.1.7, physical PDF pp. 158-161): input-on transient, full-overlap steady state, and input-off transient as the filter slides across a finite record.
Recreate overlap-add (Sec. 4.1.10, physical PDF pp. 165-167): partition a long stream, convolve each block, shift by block length, and add overlapping tails to recover the global result.
Recreate the FIR circular buffer (Sec. 4.3.4, physical PDF pp. 184-188): fixed memory cells, a rotating newest-sample pointer, and coefficient traversal showing no physical array shift.

Recreate the ROC decision atlas (Secs. 5.2-5.3, physical PDF pp. 217-223): one pole pattern with exterior, interior, and annular regions labeled causal/anticausal/two-sided and stable/unstable according to unit-circle inclusion.

Recreate pole-zero geometric frequency response (Sec. 5.4, physical PDF pp. 226-231): a point walking around the unit circle with numerator zero distances and denominator pole distances forming magnitude peaks and nulls.
Recreate switched-sinusoid response (Sec. 6.3.2, physical PDF pp. 255-260): steady sinusoid plus exponentially decaying pole modes, with epsilon settling time and input-off symmetry.

Recreate resonator/equalizer pole-zero controls (Sec. 6.4.2, physical PDF pp. 263-271): angle controls center frequency, pole radius controls bandwidth/settling, and zero radius switches boost, cut, or notch.

Recreate inverse-filter feasibility (Sec. 6.5, physical PDF pp. 274-283): minimum-phase versus outside-unit-circle zeros, causal unstable versus stable anticausal inverses, tail truncation/delay, and amplified noise.

Recreate the realization family tree (Chapter 7, physical PDF pp. 293-329): direct form I, delay-merged canonical form, transposed form, state space, and cascaded biquads, annotated with memory and numerical tradeoffs.

Recreate normalized lattice flow and recursion (Secs. 8.1-8.4, physical PDF pp. 354-370): two-port sections, reflection coefficients, tau normalization, forward/backward polynomial recursion, and ladder output taps.

Recreate the finite-word stability comparison (Secs. 8.9-8.10, physical PDF pp. 377-383): exact response and quantized direct/cascade/lattice responses beside their moved poles, emphasizing clustered-pole sensitivity.

Recreate the window tradeoff gallery (Secs. 9.1 and 9.3, physical PDF pp. 385-401): time shapes and normalized spectra for rectangular, Hamming, Kaiser, DPSS, and Chebyshev windows, aligned by 3-dB width and sidelobe level.
Recreate weak-tone detection (Example 9.3.2, physical PDF pp. 402-405): a tone 60 dB below two neighbors under each window, making leakage-driven invisibility versus detection immediately visible.

Recreate periodogram improvement paths (Sec. 9.6, physical PDF pp. 418-423): ordinary periodogram branching to K-segment/Welch averaging and to autocorrelation lag-window smoothing, with variance and resolution arrows.

Recreate random-noise filtering (Sec. 9.7, physical PDF pp. 424-426): input PSD multiplied by |H|^2, integrated to output variance/NRR, followed by accumulator variance growing linearly and the leaky-integrator fix.
gems: Example 1.4.1 (physical PDF pp. 39-40; printed pp. 16-17): a 10 Hz sinusoid sampled at only 12 Hz reconstructs as -2 Hz, turning aliasing into a single memorable arithmetic reduction.
Example 1.4.3 (physical PDF pp. 42-43; printed pp. 19-20): five analog frequencies -7, -3, 1, 5, and 9 Hz produce exactly the same samples at fs=4 Hz.
Example 1.4.4 (physical PDF pp. 43-44; printed pp. 20-21): sampling 4+3cos(pi t)+2cos(2pi t)+cos(3pi t) at half its Nyquist rate collapses distinct components into 5+5cos(pi t).

Example 1.6.1 (physical PDF pp. 65-66; printed pp. 42-43): in a 12 kHz audio chain with 2 kHz retained bandwidth and an 80 dB image target, the staircase DAC supplies 14.4 dB at the nearest image, leaving 65.6 dB for the analog postfilter.

Example 2.1.1 (physical PDF pp. 88-89; printed pp. 65-66): a 44 kHz, 10 V audio converter constrained below 50 microvolts RMS quantization noise lands at 16 bits, 44 microvolts, 704 kbit/s, and about 96 dB dynamic range.

Example 2.4.6 (physical PDF pp. 109-111; printed pp. 86-88): 1000 simulated errors with Q=1 give sigma=0.287 against Q/sqrt(12)=0.289, then histogram and correlation plots test the assumptions rather than merely asserting them.

Example 2.5.1 (physical PDF pp. 114-116; printed pp. 91-93): a 0.75-LSB sinusoid quantizes into an odd-harmonic, square-wave-like pattern; triangular dither audibly and visibly replaces the spurs with featureless noise.

Secs. 3.4-3.5 (physical PDF pp. 132-140; printed pp. 109-117): a centered five-tap smoother becomes causal with a two-sample delay, and the text generalizes the trick into a quantitative tail-clipping method for stable anticausal systems.

Example 4.1.1 and following forms (physical PDF pp. 147-157; printed pp. 124-134): the same two short sequences are carried through every convolution representation to the shared result [1,3,3,5,3,7,4,3,3,0,1].

Sec. 4.3.4 (physical PDF pp. 184-188; printed pp. 161-165): a 100 ms audio delay at 44.1 kHz needs 4410 stored samples, making the advantage of rotating an address pointer instead of copying a delay line impossible to miss.

Sec. 5.6 mortgage example (physical PDF pp. 239-241; printed pp. 216-218): a $10,000 five-year loan at 6% becomes a recurrence solved several ways, including unilateral z transform, yielding a $193.33 monthly payment and $1,599.68 total interest.

Example 6.3.2 (physical PDF pp. 258-260; printed pp. 235-237): a pole radius of 0.97 predicts a 151.2-sample 1% settling duration; a 300-sample gated sinusoid is therefore almost all input-on and input-off transient.

Example 6.4.3 (physical PDF pp. 272-274; printed pp. 249-251): at fs=600 Hz, rejecting 60 Hz and all its harmonics becomes the compact ten-notch numerator 1-z^-10 with nearby poles controlling notch width.

Sec. 6.5 (physical PDF pp. 274-283; printed pp. 251-260): the proposed ideal room processor deconvolves the listening room and then convolves a concert hall response, immediately exposing both the promise and fragility of inverse filtering.

Sec. 7.7 (physical PDF pp. 333-339; printed pp. 310-316): historical DSP32C cycle counts turn structures into hard sampling-rate limits—for example, a 100-tap FIR reaches roughly 112.4 kHz—providing a reusable real-time budgeting exercise even though the chip is obsolete.

Computer Experiments 8.10 (physical PDF pp. 378-383; printed pp. 355-360): a fourth-order double resonator becomes unstable when its direct coefficients are rounded to two digits while the cascade survives; a sixth-order Chebyshev direct form fails at four fractional digits while cascade and normalized lattice remain stable.

Example 9.2.1 (physical PDF pp. 397-398; printed pp. 374-375): a DTMF detector needs the DTFT at only eight frequencies, so selective evaluation/Goertzel beats a full FFT; the closest tone groups imply a minimum rectangular record of about 30 samples at 8 kHz.

Example 9.3.2 (physical PDF pp. 402-405; printed pp. 379-382): a middle sinusoid 60 dB below two strong neighbors is invisible under rectangular/Hamming leakage but recoverable with properly specified Kaiser, DPSS, or Chebyshev windows.

Sec. 9.7 (physical PDF pp. 425-426; printed pp. 402-403): the warning 'never accumulate or integrate white noise' is justified exactly by variance growing as (n+1)sigma_x^2, then repaired by one transparent pole-radius change.

Computer Experiment 9.8 (physical PDF pp. 426-431; printed pp. 403-408): 309 annual sunspot means from 1700-2008 expose the approximately 11-year cycle while ordinary, averaged, 50%-overlap Welch, and Bartlett-smoothed estimates make the resolution-variance tradeoff concrete.
